To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(1) Ca-dependent action potentials do not occur in regenerating cockroaches giant interneurons; (2) the degenerative process of the giant interneuron axon is retarded by ligation of the axon prior to the cut; and (3) sprouting of the giant intereneuron axon occurs at the lesion as well as at sites some distance away from the lesion.

(i) Ca-dependent action potentials were not observed in GIs; (ii) ligation of GIs before cutting delayed the degenerative response of the axon; (iii) cutting GIs at various distances from their cell body produced similar responses, suggesting that there was no correlation between the response of the cell body and that of the axon.
In summary, our research is concerned with
a possible role for calcium in the generation of transient action potentials in cockroach GIs.
a number of problems related to the regeneration of the axon of cockroach GIs.
the effects of axotomy on the electrophysiology and morphology of cockroach giant internerones.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
there is no evidence for the transient, Ca2+ dependent, action potentials reported previously.
no consistent pattern of growth and regeneration was found in the regenerating GIs of cockroaches.
there are no changes in the electrophysiology of GIs which can be related directly to the site of the injury, but that there are some changes which are related to the injury.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the Ca-dependent, transient, action potentials are not a general property of regenerating cockroach GIs.
the transient Ca-dependent action potentials are not a normal feature of GIs.
, in cockroach GIs, the injury response is not dependent on the distance from the site of the cell body.
The main takeaway from our work is that
there is no evidence for the existence of transient Ca-dependent action potentials at the tips of GIs.
the Ca-dependent transient potential reported by Meiri et al. is not an injury potential and is not related to the lesion site.
there was no clear relation between the site of the injury and the site of sprouting, nor were the transient action potentials seen near the tip of the GI.
